title: start with the person in the mirror
hookLine: start with the person in the mirror
tomorrow: do something for someone with no receipt

lines: WHAT YOU SAY TO A FRIEND.
cards: A friend burns the dinner. Misses a deadline. Says the wrong thing at the wrong moment.
What comes out of your mouth? Usually something like: hey, it happens, you're tired, it's fine. Now flip it.
You burn the dinner. What does the voice inside say then? Sometimes it's a voice nobody would be allowed to use on a friend.
Idiot. Of course you did. Typical.

teach.b: In the early Buddhist teachings there's a word, metta. It's usually translated loving-kindness, but it comes from the Pali word for friend. Metta is friendliness: wanting good for someone the way a friend does.

One short Buddhist discourse describes it with a picture: the way a mother would protect her only child with her own life, a person can grow a heart like that toward every living being. Here's the surprise.
The Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa wrote a long guide to meditation, and when he explains how to practice metta, he says not to start with everyone.

Start with yourself. Wish yourself well first, with phrases like may I be happy, may I be free from trouble. Then extend it outward: to someone dear, to someone neutral, and eventually to someone difficult.
His reasoning is plain. You know from the inside that you want to be happy. That makes you the example: everyone else wants the same.

Remember yesterday's line from the Hebrew Bible: "love thy neighbour as thyself." Those last two words carry a quiet assumption: that there's some care for yourself to measure by. Modern research points somewhere similar.
The psychologist Kristin Neff studies self-compassion: treating your own failures the way you'd treat a friend's. A common worry is that being kind to yourself will make you lazy.

teach.h: GENTLE WITH MISTAKES, MORE LIKELY TO TRY.
teach.b: In one set of studies, people nudged to be gentler about a mistake were more willing to own it, and put more effort into doing better. Some people feel they don't even deserve to sit, because of something they've done.
If that's you: feeling bad about harm means your conscience works, and practice is how people learn to do less of it. Kindness isn't a reward for getting it right. It's where you start.

how: In Buddhist loving-kindness (metta) meditation, practitioners often begin by silently wishing themselves well with a few short phrases, then extend the same wishes to a friend, a stranger, a difficult person and finally all beings.

games.q: you're learning metta from Buddhaghosa's guide. who do you wish well first?
o: someone difficult, to get the hard part over.
games.why: yourself. then someone dear, someone neutral, and in time someone difficult. you know you want to be happy, so you become the example for everyone else.

practice: Here's the practice. The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle.
Then picture yourself the way a good friend might see you right now: tired, trying, doing your best with the day you've had. On each breath out, say quietly inside: may I be at ease.
If it feels strange or even a little silly, that's normal. Say it anyway.

wordCard.voice: Kindness. Wanting good for someone the way a friend does, starting with the one in the mirror. Sixteenth word.

orig.note: Pali, from the Buddhist tradition: friendliness, loving-kindness. It comes from mitta, friend (Sanskrit maitrī).

carryVoice: Your line: may I be at ease. It's the sentence you'd give a friend, turned around. Day sixteen.
